Chapter 4: The Impact of Racism on Young People and Their Communities
For a lot of kids and teens, racism isn’t just some far-off idea—it’s something they experience every day.
It shows up in the classroom, like when teachers seem to call on some students more than others, or in the way a joke slips through in the hallway without anyone batting an eye.
Even the rules and expectations can feel different, depending on who you are. Over time, these moments aren’t just blips—they shape how young people see the world, and even how they see themselves.
Imagine a high schooler raising her hand, but the teacher looks past her again and again.
She might start to wonder—is it because of her accent, her hair, or the color of her skin?
In another class, maybe a boy gets in trouble for something his friends do too, but the consequences seem a lot harsher for him.
After a while, he learns to keep his head down, to avoid attention, and to expect less from the people around him.
These little slights—what people often call microaggressions—might seem tiny when they happen on their own.
But think about it: when they happen over and over, they really add up.
A student who’s always being asked, “Where are you really from?” starts to feel like he doesn’t belong.
Or a girl hears, “You’re pretty for a Black girl,” and realizes that someone else’s idea of beauty is being put above her own.
The message is loud and clear—you’re different, and that’s somehow a problem.
This kind of treatment takes a toll.
Some young people pull back—they lose interest in school or the activities they used to love.
Others might get angry or start acting out, frustrated with a system that feels rigged against them.
And sometimes, they start believing those negative messages, doubting their abilities and their worth.
It’s not just the individuals who feel it—whole communities are affected.
When students of color get stuck in lower-level classes or miss out on opportunities, everyone loses.
Talents go unrecognized, relationships get strained, and trust between families and schools starts to crack.
Parents notice when their kids come home discouraged or when their concerns aren't taken seriously by teachers.
That sense of belonging, which is so important for learning, starts to slip away.
But here’s something inspiring—even with these challenges, so many young people find ways to push back and shine.
They look for mentors who truly believe in them, join clubs that celebrate who they are, or connect with friends who get it.
In some schools, students organize for more inclusive lessons or to call out unfair rules.
These acts of resistance aren’t just about getting by—they’re about standing tall and claiming dignity.
And adults really matter here.
A teacher who takes the time to learn about a student’s background, who listens without judging, can make a huge difference.
A parent who lifts up their child’s identity and helps them navigate what it means to grow up in a world full of challenges gives them real strength.
Even the smallest gestures—a kind word, a listening ear—can help undo some of those negative messages.
The effects of racism aren’t just about one person—they ripple out to everyone.
When one student is left out, the whole community misses out on their unique gifts and perspective.
Tackling these issues takes more than just good intentions.
It calls for a real commitment to fairness, honesty, and always looking for ways to do better.
Sure, the work is tough—but building a more just and welcoming community is absolutely worth it.
